walkthroughs.body_html:
Coastal Landscapes / Glaciated Landscapes / Dryland Landscapes — a core area of A-Level Geography.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Coastal Landscapes / Glaciated Landscapes / Dryland Landscapes brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

mcqs.q: What are the three cells of global atmospheric circulation?
options: The Hadley cell (equator to 30 degrees), Ferrel cell (30 to 60 degrees) and Polar cell (60 degrees to poles) together redistribute heat from equator to poles.
There is one big Hadley cell from the equator to each pole.
Primary effects happen first and secondary effects happen the next day.
The three cells are tropical, temperate and arctic, named after climate zones.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between primary and secondary effects of an earthquake?
options: Primary effects occur immediately as a direct result of shaking (building collapse, deaths); secondary effects follow afterwards (fires, tsunamis, disease, homelessness).
The three cells are tropical, temperate and arctic, named after climate zones.
Primary effects happen first and secondary effects happen the next day.
Primary effects are the worst effects and secondary effects are minor.

mcqs.q: Why has the Richter scale been largely replaced by the moment magnitude scale?
options: The Richter scale is still the standard scale used by all seismologists.
The three cells are tropical, temperate and arctic, named after climate zones.
Moment magnitude measures damage while Richter measures shaking.
Richter saturates above magnitude ~7 and was calibrated for local Californian quakes; moment magnitude (Mw) measures the total energy released and works for all sizes globally.
